questions.s: An 18-month-old girl, Ayesha, is brought to a BHU with fever of 39 °C and irritability for 2 days. She keeps pulling at both ears. Otoscopy shows red, bulging tympanic membranes on both sides with no discharge. She is otherwise well hydrated and has no allergies. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Bilateral acute otitis media in a child under 2 years is an indication for an oral antibiotic, and amoxicillin is first line because it covers pneumococcus and Haemophilus. Ear drops do not treat middle ear infection behind an intact drum, and ciprofloxacin is not a first-line oral agent for children. Myringotomy is reserved for complications or failed treatment.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy in Multan has had poor hearing at school for 4 months since a cold. He has no ear pain or fever. Otoscopy shows dull, retracted tympanic membranes with an air–fluid level behind them. Tympanometry gives a flat (type B) trace on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A painless conductive hearing loss in a child with a dull, retracted drum, fluid level and flat tympanogram is otitis media with effusion (glue ear). Acute otitis media causes pain, fever and a bulging red drum. Chronic suppurative otitis media needs a perforation with discharge, and otosclerosis presents in young adults with a normal drum.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man has had a scanty, foul-smelling discharge from his left ear for 3 years with gradually worsening hearing. Otoscopy shows a posterosuperior marginal (attic) perforation with white flakes of debris. Pure tone audiometry shows a 35 dB conductive loss on the left. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Myringoplasty with a temporalis fascia graft
Mastoid surgery to remove the disease
questions.e: An attic or marginal perforation with white keratin debris and foul discharge indicates cholesteatoma, which erodes bone and can cause intracranial complications, so it needs surgical removal by mastoid surgery. Drops may reduce discharge but do not remove keratin. Myringoplasty alone suits a dry central perforation of the safe type, not cholesteatoma.

questions.s: A 5-year-old boy had a painful ear for a week treated by a local pharmacist. Now he has high fever and a tender, fluctuant swelling behind the right ear that pushes the pinna forward and downward. The postauricular skin crease is obliterated. The drum is red and bulging. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A postauricular fluctuant swelling that displaces the pinna forward and downward, with an obliterated postauricular crease after otitis media, is acute mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess. Lymphadenitis and a furuncle can cause postauricular swelling but the crease is usually preserved and the drum is normal. The child needs admission, IV antibiotics and imaging.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has had severe left ear pain worse at night for 6 weeks despite ear drops. There is granulation tissue in the floor of the ear canal at the bony–cartilaginous junction. He has now developed a left lower motor neurone facial weakness. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Severe otalgia with canal-floor granulations and cranial nerve palsy in an elderly diabetic is necrotising (malignant) otitis externa, a skull base osteomyelitis almost always caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Staphylococcus causes furunculosis, Aspergillus causes otomycosis with fungal debris, and pneumococcus causes acute otitis media.

questions.s: A 30-year-old swimmer presents with ear pain and itching for 3 days. Pulling on the pinna and pressing the tragus are very painful. The ear canal is swollen and red with moist debris, and the drum is intact where seen. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Topical antibiotic drops with aural toilet
Myringotomy and insertion of a ventilation tube
questions.e: Pain on moving the pinna or pressing the tragus with a swollen, moist canal is acute otitis externa, which is treated by cleaning the canal and topical antibiotic (often with steroid) drops. Oral antibiotics are needed only for spreading cellulitis or immunosuppression. Myringotomy is for middle ear disease, which this is not.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has a painless, intermittent mucoid discharge from her right ear after colds. Otoscopy between episodes shows a dry central perforation of the pars tensa with a healthy middle ear mucosa. Audiometry shows a 25 dB conductive loss. She wants the ear to be dry permanently. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A dry central perforation of the pars tensa with intermittent mucoid discharge is tubotympanic (mucosal, safe) chronic suppurative otitis media, and closing the perforation with myringoplasty stops recurrent infection. Mastoid surgery is needed for cholesteatoma. Long-term drops do not close the perforation and some are ototoxic.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has gradually worsening hearing in both ears for 3 years, worse since her recent pregnancy. Her mother wore a hearing aid from age 40. She says she hears better in noisy places. Both drums look normal. Rinne test is negative on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss in a young woman with normal drums, a family history, worsening in pregnancy and better hearing in noise (paracusis Willisii) points to otosclerosis with stapes fixation. Glue ear shows an abnormal drum, presbycusis is sensorineural in older people, and Ménière disease causes fluctuating sensorineural loss with vertigo.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man complains of reduced hearing in his right ear. With a 512 Hz tuning fork, Rinne test is positive on both sides and Weber test lateralises to the left ear. What type of hearing loss does this show?
questions.e: Rinne positive on both sides means air conduction is better than bone conduction, so there is no significant conductive loss. Weber lateralises away from an ear with sensorineural loss towards the better cochlea, so a left-sided Weber with right-sided complaints means right sensorineural loss. In right conductive loss Weber would go to the right and right Rinne would be negative.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has worked for 20 years in a textile weaving mill in Faisalabad without ear protection. He has trouble hearing conversation and has ringing in both ears. Otoscopy is normal. What finding on pure tone audiometry is most typical of his condition?
o: Low-frequency loss with an upsloping curve
Bilateral dip in hearing around 4 kHz
Air–bone gap of 30 dB at all frequencies
Dip in bone conduction around 2 kHz
questions.e: Chronic noise exposure damages outer hair cells in the basal cochlea, giving a bilateral sensorineural notch around 4 kHz with recovery at 8 kHz. A low-frequency upsloping loss suggests Ménière disease, an air–bone gap means conductive loss, and a bone-conduction dip at 2 kHz is the Carhart notch of otosclerosis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old teacher woke 2 days ago with sudden loss of hearing in her left ear and tinnitus. There is no vertigo, pain or discharge. Otoscopy is normal. Weber lateralises to the right and Rinne is positive on both sides. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Fit a hearing aid in the left ear
Reassure and repeat audiometry in 3 months
questions.e: Normal otoscopy with Weber going to the opposite ear indicates sudden sensorineural hearing loss, an otological emergency; after confirming with urgent audiometry, early high-dose oral steroids give the best chance of recovery, and an MRI is arranged later to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. Waiting or fitting a hearing aid loses the window for treatment, and syringing is for wax, which otoscopy has excluded.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man on treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis receives a daily injectable agent for several months. He develops tinnitus and difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds. Which drug in his regimen is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Aminoglycosides such as amikacin, streptomycin and kanamycin are toxic to cochlear hair cells, causing permanent high-frequency sensorineural loss, which is why monthly audiometry is done when they are used. Linezolid causes neuropathy and myelosuppression, levofloxacin tendon problems and QT prolongation, and clofazimine skin discolouration.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has brief spells of spinning vertigo lasting less than a minute whenever she turns over in bed or looks up to a high shelf. Hearing is normal. With her head turned to the right and quickly lowered below the couch, torsional upbeating nystagmus appears after a few seconds and fades. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral betahistine three times daily for 3 months
questions.e: Short positional vertigo with a positive Dix–Hallpike test on the right is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the right posterior canal, treated by the Epley manoeuvre that moves otoconia out of the canal. Vestibular sedatives only mask symptoms and delay compensation. Betahistine and intratympanic gentamicin are used in Ménière disease.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man has had several attacks over 6 months of spinning vertigo lasting 2 to 4 hours, with nausea, roaring tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the right ear. Between attacks he is well but hearing in that ear is worse each time. Audiometry shows a right low-frequency sensorineural loss. What is the underlying pathology?
o: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
questions.e: Episodic vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is Ménière disease, caused by excess endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops). Otoconia cause seconds-long positional vertigo, vestibular neuritis causes one prolonged attack without hearing loss, and a schwannoma causes slowly progressive unilateral loss rather than discrete attacks.

questions.s: A 33-year-old woman had a cold last week. Yesterday she developed continuous severe spinning vertigo with vomiting. She can walk with help. Hearing is normal. There is horizontal nystagmus beating to the left, and the head impulse test shows a corrective saccade when the head is turned to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute continuous vertigo after a viral illness, normal hearing, unidirectional nystagmus beating away from the affected side and an abnormal head impulse test to the right indicate right vestibular neuritis. An abnormal head impulse is reassuring because it points to a peripheral lesion; in cerebellar stroke the head impulse is usually normal. BPPV and Ménière disease cause episodic, not continuous, vertigo.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has had progressive hearing loss and tinnitus in his left ear only for 2 years, with mild unsteadiness. Examination shows reduced left corneal reflex. Audiometry shows a left sensorineural loss with poor speech discrimination. What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Non-contrast CT scan of the paranasal sinuses
MRI of the internal acoustic meatus
questions.e: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus, poor speech discrimination and a reduced corneal reflex (trigeminal involvement) suggests a vestibular schwannoma in the cerebellopontine angle, and gadolinium MRI of the internal acoustic meatus is the investigation of choice. Tympanometry assesses the middle ear, which is not the problem here, and a sinus CT does not image the cerebellopontine angle.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man woke with inability to close his right eye and drooping of the right side of his mouth. He cannot wrinkle the right side of his forehead. There are no vesicles on the ear, no limb weakness and ear examination is normal. Symptoms began 24 hours ago. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Urgent surgical decompression of the facial nerve
questions.e: An isolated lower motor neurone facial palsy of sudden onset with normal ears is Bell palsy, and oral prednisolone started within 72 hours improves recovery, together with eye care to prevent corneal exposure. Aciclovir alone is not effective and antivirals are added mainly when vesicles suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Surgical decompression is not routine.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy has a nosebleed from the right nostril while playing cricket in the heat. He is otherwise well with no bleeding history. Blood is trickling from the front of the nose. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Sit him leaning forward and pinch the soft nose
Lie him flat and pack the nose with gauze
Tilt his head back and apply ice to the neck
Cauterise the septum with silver nitrate
questions.e: Most nosebleeds in young people come from Little's area on the anterior septum, and the first step is to sit leaning forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes. Tilting the head back makes the patient swallow blood and hides ongoing bleeding. Cautery or packing is used if first aid fails.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy has had progressive right nasal obstruction for a year and several episodes of heavy, unprovoked bleeding from the right nostril. Nasal endoscopy shows a smooth, red, lobulated mass in the posterior nasal cavity. CT shows the mass widening the pterygopalatine fossa with forward bowing of the posterior maxillary wall. What should be avoided in his management?
o: Biopsy of the mass in clinic
questions.e: An adolescent male with nasal obstruction, recurrent profuse epistaxis and a vascular mass widening the pterygopalatine fossa has juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Clinic biopsy can cause torrential haemorrhage, so diagnosis is made on imaging, and surgery is planned with angiography and embolisation. Checking haemoglobin and cross-match is appropriate preparation.

questions.s: A 70-year-old hypertensive man has brisk bleeding from both nostrils and into the throat for 2 hours. Pinching the nose does not help, and anterior rhinoscopy after suction shows no bleeding point on the septum. BP is 170/100 mmHg and pulse 104/min. An anterior nasal pack fails to stop blood running down the pharynx. Which artery is most likely bleeding?
questions.e: Posterior epistaxis in an older hypertensive patient, with blood running into the pharynx despite an anterior pack and no anterior bleeding point, usually comes from branches of the sphenopalatine artery. The superior labial and greater palatine arteries supply Little's area anteriorly, and the anterior ethmoidal artery bleeds from high in the nose, typically after trauma.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has had recurrent nosebleeds since her teens and now has iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 8.9 g/dL). Her father had the same problem. Examination shows small red spots on her lips, tongue and fingertips that blanch with pressure. Platelet count and clotting are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias on lips, tongue and fingers and autosomal dominant inheritance with normal coagulation tests are typical of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Von Willebrand disease usually prolongs the bleeding time or APTT and does not cause telangiectasia, and immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man was punched on the nose 2 days ago. He now has severe bilateral nasal obstruction. Examination shows a soft, fluctuant, dusky swelling on both sides of the nasal septum. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Review in 7 days for reduction of the fracture
Anterior nasal packing with ribbon gauze
Urgent incision and drainage of the swelling
questions.e: A bilateral, fluctuant septal swelling after trauma is a septal haematoma, which separates the cartilage from its blood supply; it needs urgent incision and drainage to prevent abscess, cartilage necrosis and saddle nose. Waiting a week is the plan for a simple nasal bone deformity, not for a haematoma. Decongestants and antibiotics alone do not drain the blood.

questions.s: A 7-year-old girl has had a cold for a week. She now has fever, painful swelling and redness of the left upper and lower eyelids, proptosis and painful, restricted eye movements. Visual acuity is reduced on the left. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav at home with review by the GP in 48 hours
Admission, IV antibiotics and CT of orbits and sinuses
questions.e: Proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia and reduced vision after a cold indicate orbital (post-septal) cellulitis, usually spreading from ethmoid sinusitis in children. It needs admission, IV antibiotics and urgent CT to find a subperiosteal abscess that may need drainage. Oral antibiotics are appropriate only for preseptal cellulitis without eye signs.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has had bilateral nasal blockage and loss of smell for a year. Anterior rhinoscopy shows smooth, pale grey, glistening masses in both nasal cavities that are insensitive to probing and move easily. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Bilateral pale, insensitive, mobile masses with anosmia are nasal polyps of chronic rhinosinusitis, and the first-line treatment is a topical intranasal corticosteroid, with surgery if this fails. Antihistamines do not shrink polyps, and long-term decongestant sprays cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman is admitted to a teaching hospital in Karachi with diabetic ketoacidosis. On day 2 she develops left facial pain and swelling. Examination shows a black, necrotic patch on the left inferior turbinate and the hard palate. What is the most appropriate management in addition to correcting the ketoacidosis?
o: IV amphotericin B and surgical debridement
Nasal saline irrigation and steroid spray
questions.e: Black necrotic eschar of the nose or palate in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis is invasive mucormycosis, which spreads along blood vessels and is fatal without urgent IV amphotericin B and radical surgical debridement. Fluconazole has no activity against Mucorales, and antibacterial antibiotics do not treat a fungal infection.

questions.s: A 16-year-old girl, Mehwish, presents with fever, severe sore throat and pain on swallowing for 2 days. She has no cough. Her tonsils are swollen with white exudate and the anterior cervical nodes are tender. She has no drug allergies. What is the most appropriate antibiotic?
o: Oral co-trimoxazole twice daily for 3 days
questions.e: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and no cough suggest group A streptococcal tonsillitis, and penicillin V for 10 days is first line to eradicate the organism and prevent rheumatic fever. Ciprofloxacin and co-trimoxazole are poor choices for streptococci, and vancomycin is reserved for serious resistant infections.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has had a sore throat for 5 days that has become much worse on the left. He has a muffled voice, drools because swallowing hurts, and can open his mouth only 2 cm. The left soft palate bulges and the uvula is pushed to the right. Temperature is 38.6 °C. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral amoxicillin at home and review in the clinic in a week
Needle aspiration or incision with IV antibiotics
questions.e: Trismus, a hot-potato voice, unilateral palatal bulge and uvula deviation after tonsillitis indicate a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). It is treated by draining the pus by needle aspiration or incision plus IV antibiotics and fluids. Oral antibiotics alone are inadequate, and immediate tonsillectomy is not the standard first step.

questions.s: An unvaccinated 5-year-old boy from a village in Balochistan has fever, sore throat and a markedly swollen neck. A greyish-white membrane covers both tonsils and extends onto the soft palate; it bleeds when the edge is lifted. What is the most important immediate treatment besides isolation?
questions.e: An adherent grey membrane spreading beyond the tonsils that bleeds on removal, with a bull neck in an unvaccinated child, is faucial diphtheria. Antitoxin should be given as early as possible on clinical suspicion because it neutralises circulating toxin before it binds to the heart and nerves, and penicillin or erythromycin eradicates the organism. Antibiotics alone do not neutralise toxin.

questions.s: A 19-year-old university student has fever, sore throat and marked fatigue for a week. Examination shows enlarged tonsils with exudate, palatal petechiae, tender posterior cervical nodes and a palpable spleen. A clinic doctor prescribed amoxicillin 2 days ago and he now has a widespread itchy maculopapular rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Exudative tonsillitis with posterior cervical nodes, palatal petechiae, splenomegaly and fatigue in a young adult is infectious mononucleosis, and a rash after amoxicillin is a well-known reaction in EBV infection that does not mean true penicillin allergy. Streptococcal tonsillitis does not cause splenomegaly. He should avoid contact sports while the spleen is enlarged.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy had a tonsillectomy 7 days ago. He is brought back with bright red bleeding from the mouth since the morning, fever of 38.2 °C and a foul smell. Pulse is 118/min. The tonsil bed is covered with slough with a slow ooze of blood. What is the most likely cause of this bleeding?
o: Slipped ligature on the tonsillar artery
Damage to the internal carotid artery
questions.e: Bleeding 5 to 10 days after tonsillectomy is secondary haemorrhage, usually caused by infection of the tonsillar bed, shown here by fever, slough and foul smell; it is managed with admission, IV antibiotics and fluids, and return to theatre if it does not settle. A slipped ligature causes reactionary bleeding within 24 hours. A coagulation disorder would usually show at surgery.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl snores loudly every night, with pauses in breathing that her mother has noticed, restless sleep and daytime irritability. She breathes through her mouth. Examination shows very large tonsils that nearly meet in the midline. Growth is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Snoring with witnessed apnoeas and daytime behaviour problems in a child with large tonsils indicates obstructive sleep apnoea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy, and adenotonsillectomy is the main treatment. Antibiotics do not reduce lymphoid hypertrophy, and weight reduction is relevant when obesity is the cause, which it is not here.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy has had fever for 4 days and now refuses to eat, drools and holds his neck stiffly, avoiding turning it. He has noisy breathing. There is a bulge on the posterior pharyngeal wall to one side of the midline. What would a lateral soft tissue X-ray of the neck most likely show?
questions.e: Fever, drooling, neck stiffness and a unilateral bulge of the posterior pharyngeal wall in a child under 5 indicate a retropharyngeal abscess, which widens the prevertebral soft tissue shadow on a lateral neck X-ray. The thumb sign suggests epiglottitis and the steeple sign is seen on an AP film in croup.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man had pain in a decayed lower molar for a week. He now has fever, a tense, woody, tender swelling under the chin on both sides, his tongue is pushed up and back, and he speaks with difficulty. What is the main danger in this condition?
questions.e: Bilateral brawny submandibular swelling with elevation of the tongue after a lower molar infection is Ludwig angina, a cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces. Its main danger is rapid airway obstruction, so the airway is secured early, alongside IV antibiotics and drainage. Cavernous sinus thrombosis follows infection of the upper face, not the floor of the mouth.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy has had a runny nose for 2 days and tonight developed a harsh barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor when crying, but not at rest. Temperature is 37.9 °C. He is alert, playful and not drooling. Oxygen saturation is 97 % in air. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: A barking cough, hoarseness and stridor after coryza in a well toddler is croup, usually caused by parainfluenza virus. A single dose of oral dexamethasone reduces airway swelling and is given for all severities; nebulised adrenaline is added for severe stridor at rest. Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, not subglottic oedema.

questions.s: An unvaccinated 4-year-old girl has had high fever for 6 hours. She looks toxic, sits leaning forward with her mouth open and drools saliva. She has a soft inspiratory stridor and a muffled voice but no cough. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Send her for a lateral neck X-ray
Lie her flat and insert an IV cannula
Keep her calm and call senior airway help
questions.e: A toxic, drooling child sitting forward with stridor and no cough has acute epiglottitis, usually from Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children. Distressing her by examining the throat, lying her flat or sending her away for X-ray can cause complete obstruction, so she is kept calm with a parent while an experienced anaesthetist and ENT surgeon secure the airway.

questions.s: A 6-week-old baby has had noisy breathing since the second week of life. The noise is a high-pitched inspiratory stridor, worse when he feeds, cries or lies on his back, and better when prone. He is feeding well and gaining weight. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in infants: inspiratory stridor from the early weeks, worse supine and with feeding, in a thriving baby, caused by floppy supraglottic tissues that usually settle by 18 to 24 months. Bilateral cord palsy usually causes stridor from birth and is often linked to neurological problems, and a vascular ring causes biphasic stridor with feeding difficulty.

questions.s: A 46-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy yesterday. Today her voice is weak and breathy, and she coughs when drinking water. Breathing is comfortable with no stridor. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord fixed near the midline. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
questions.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and runs close to the inferior thyroid artery, so injury at thyroidectomy causes an immobile cord, a weak breathy voice and aspiration. External laryngeal nerve injury affects cricothyroid, causing loss of high pitch and voice fatigue with mobile cords.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man had a tracheostomy 4 days ago. The nurse calls because he is suddenly distressed, with noisy breathing and falling oxygen saturation. There is no air flow through the tube. He has a cuffed tube with an inner cannula. What should be done first?
o: Remove the outer tube and re-intubate orally
Give a sedative and increase the oxygen
Instil saline and wait for a cough
questions.e: Sudden obstruction of a recent tracheostomy is most often caused by secretions in the tube, and the first step is to remove the inner cannula, which clears a blocked lumen at once, then pass a suction catheter. Removing the whole tube in the first week is risky because the tract is not yet formed. Sedation worsens hypoventilation.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman is having a severe allergic reaction after a wasp sting. Despite IM adrenaline, her lips and tongue are massively swollen and attempts at oral intubation and mask ventilation have failed. Oxygen saturation is 70 % and falling. What is the most appropriate immediate airway procedure?
questions.e: In a 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' situation the emergency front-of-neck airway is a cricothyroidotomy through the cricothyroid membrane, which is superficial and quick to reach. A formal tracheostomy takes too long in a crash setting, and repeated intubation attempts waste time and worsen swelling. A nasopharyngeal airway will not bypass laryngeal oedema.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man with hypertension has developed swelling of his lips and tongue over 2 hours without itching or urticaria. He started a new tablet for blood pressure 3 weeks ago. He has no wheeze. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril cause bradykinin-mediated angioedema of the lips, tongue and larynx without urticaria or itch, and it can occur weeks to years after starting. The drug must be stopped permanently and the airway watched closely. Amlodipine causes ankle oedema, which is a different mechanism.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy is brought because his mother saw him push something into his right ear. Otoscopy shows a dried chickpea in the outer part of the ear canal. The drum cannot be seen. What should be avoided?
o: Removal with a fine hook under good light
Removal under general anaesthesia if he struggles
Referral to an ENT clinic for microscope removal
questions.e: Vegetable foreign bodies such as chickpeas or beans absorb water and swell when syringed, becoming impacted and painful, so syringing should be avoided. They are removed with a hook under direct vision, under a microscope by ENT, or under general anaesthesia in an uncooperative child.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy has had a foul-smelling, blood-stained discharge from the left nostril only for 2 weeks. He is otherwise well and the right nostril is clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Unilateral, foul-smelling, sometimes blood-stained nasal discharge in a young child is a foreign body until proven otherwise. Sinusitis, allergic rhinitis and adenoid enlargement usually cause bilateral symptoms. The object should be removed promptly to prevent inhalation and local damage.

questions.s: A 2-year-old girl was seen putting a small round object in her mouth 1 hour ago and vomited once. A chest X-ray shows a round radio-opaque object at the level of the upper oesophagus with a double-ring (halo) outline. She is drooling. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Give a laxative and check the stools
questions.e: A double-ring outline distinguishes a button battery from a coin, and a battery lodged in the oesophagus causes liquefactive burns within hours that can perforate into the trachea or aorta, so it needs emergency endoscopic removal. Waiting for passage is only acceptable for coins or a battery that is already beyond the oesophagus in a symptom-free child. Inducing vomiting is unsafe.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy choked while eating peanuts 3 days ago and has coughed since. He now has a wheeze heard only over the right side of the chest with reduced breath sounds there. An expiratory chest X-ray shows the right lung stays inflated while the left empties. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral antibiotics and review in a week
questions.e: A choking episode followed by unilateral wheeze and air trapping on an expiratory film indicates an inhaled foreign body acting as a ball valve, most often in the right main bronchus, which is wider and more vertical. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia removes it. Physiotherapy can dislodge the object into the trachea and cause complete obstruction.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man felt something stick in his throat while eating fish curry 3 hours ago. He points to the right side of the throat above the hyoid and has pain on swallowing. He is breathing normally. What is the most likely site of the fish bone?
o: Right tonsil or base of tongue
questions.e: Sharp fish bones commonly lodge in the tonsil, base of tongue or vallecula, and a patient who localises the sensation above the hyoid usually has the bone in the oropharynx, where it can be seen and removed. Bones that pass lower tend to stick at the cricopharyngeus, and patients localise those less accurately.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl woke screaming with a buzzing noise and pain in her left ear. Otoscopy shows a live insect moving in the ear canal. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Grasp the insect with crocodile forceps
Instil mineral oil to kill the insect
Syringe the ear with cold water
questions.e: A live insect in the ear canal is first killed by filling the canal with oil (or lidocaine), which stops it moving and stinging and reduces pain, and it is then removed. Trying to grasp a moving insect often breaks it and can injure the drum. Antibiotics do not address the problem.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man from Karachi presents with a painless lump in the right upper neck for 2 months and blocked right ear. He has no ear pain. Otoscopy shows a dull right drum with fluid behind it. The left ear is normal. Which investigation is most important?
o: Ultrasound of the thyroid and salivary glands
questions.e: A new unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult, especially with an upper neck node, suggests a nasopharyngeal carcinoma blocking the Eustachian tube, and endoscopy of the nasopharynx with biopsy of any lesion is essential. Grommet insertion without examining the postnasal space would miss the cancer.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man who has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years has had a hoarse voice for 2 months. He has no sore throat and his neck is normal on palpation. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks in a smoker must be investigated for laryngeal carcinoma by direct examination of the larynx with laryngoscopy. Voice rest or empirical treatment for reflux or infection delays diagnosis. Glottic cancers cause hoarseness early, so prompt assessment allows treatment at a curable stage.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man from rural Sindh has chewed betel quid with tobacco for 30 years. He has a painless ulcer with raised, indurated edges on the left buccal mucosa for 6 weeks that bleeds on touch. There is a hard left submandibular node. What is the most likely histological type of this lesion?
questions.e: Chewing betel quid and tobacco is the main risk factor for oral cancer in Pakistan, and the buccal mucosa is a common site; an indurated ulcer with rolled edges and a hard node is squamous cell carcinoma, which forms over 90 % of oral cancers. Adenoid cystic carcinoma arises from salivary glands, and basal cell carcinoma affects skin, not mucosa.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has a painless, slowly growing lump in front of her right ear for 3 years. It is firm, mobile and nodular. Facial nerve function is normal and there are no neck nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common parotid tumour, typically a slow-growing, painless, firm mobile lump in a middle-aged person with a normal facial nerve. Warthin tumour is commoner in older male smokers and may be bilateral. Facial weakness, pain or rapid growth would suggest malignancy such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

questions.s: A newborn baby on the postnatal ward in a Lahore hospital is due for hearing screening before discharge. Her mother asks how it is done. Which test is most commonly used as the first screening test in a well newborn?
questions.e: Automated otoacoustic emission testing is quick, painless and done in a sleeping baby, detecting the echo produced by healthy outer hair cells; automated auditory brainstem response is used if it is absent. Pure tone audiometry needs a cooperative older child, and distraction testing is used at around 7 to 9 months.

questions.s: A 72-year-old retired clerk finds it hard to follow conversation at family gatherings and turns the television up loud. He has no vertigo or ear discharge. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows a symmetrical sensorineural loss that worsens steadily towards the high frequencies. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Symmetrical, gradually progressive high-frequency sensorineural loss in an older adult is presbycusis, and hearing aids are the first-line treatment. Stapedotomy corrects the conductive loss of otosclerosis, steroids are used for sudden sensorineural loss, and cochlear implants are reserved for severe to profound loss not helped by aids.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man suddenly developed severe vertigo and vomiting 3 hours ago. He cannot stand without support. Hearing is unchanged. The nystagmus beats to the right on right gaze and to the left on left gaze. The head impulse test is normal on both sides, and there is a vertical skew deviation. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Urgent brain MRI with diffusion imaging
Oral prednisolone and review in the clinic in a week
questions.e: Direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation and a normal head impulse test (a 'dangerous' HINTS pattern) in acute vestibular syndrome point to a posterior circulation stroke rather than vestibular neuritis. He needs urgent brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and stroke care. Steroids are sometimes used in vestibular neuritis, and the Epley manoeuvre treats BPPV.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has a painful rash of small vesicles in her left ear canal and on the concha, with left lower motor neurone facial weakness and left-sided hearing loss with vertigo that began 2 days ago. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Vesicles in the ear with facial palsy and vestibulocochlear symptoms are Ramsay Hunt syndrome, reactivation of varicella zoster in the geniculate ganglion. It is treated with an antiviral such as aciclovir together with prednisolone, started early, because the prognosis is worse than in Bell palsy. Steroid alone is the standard for Bell palsy, not zoster.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman is admitted in Rawalpindi on day 5 of a febrile illness with severe body aches. She has continuous bleeding from the nose and gums. Hb 13.8 g/dL, platelets 18 × 10⁹/L (150–400), haematocrit rising. Dengue NS1 antigen is positive. Pressure on the nose slows but does not stop the bleeding. What is the main underlying cause of her epistaxis?
questions.e: Dengue causes marked thrombocytopenia and capillary leak, and mucosal bleeding from the nose and gums is a warning sign in the critical phase. Her blood pressure is not raised and nothing suggests vitamin K deficiency. Management is careful fluid therapy, local measures and nasal packing if needed, with platelet transfusion reserved for significant bleeding.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation has had anterior epistaxis from the right side for an hour. First aid with firm pressure for 15 minutes has failed, and examination after suction shows an oozing vessel on the right anterior septum. INR is 2.6 (target 2–3). What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop warfarin and give intravenous vitamin K
Silver nitrate cautery of the vessel
questions.e: A visible anterior bleeding point that persists after first aid is treated with silver nitrate cautery, applied to one side of the septum only, and an anterior pack if cautery fails. His INR is in the therapeutic range, so stopping warfarin is not needed and would expose him to stroke risk. Posterior packing and arterial ligation are for posterior bleeding.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man in Islamabad has sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, itchy nose and eyes and nasal blockage every spring, especially when the paper mulberry trees release pollen. The nasal mucosa is pale and swollen. Oral antihistamines help only partly. What is the most effective next treatment?
o: Oxymetazoline nasal drops for a month
questions.e: Seasonal sneezing, itching, watery discharge and pale boggy mucosa during the pollen season is allergic rhinitis, and a regular intranasal corticosteroid is the most effective single treatment for nasal symptoms including blockage. A month of decongestant drops causes rebound congestion, and long courses of oral steroids carry systemic risks. Surgery is for persistent blockage despite medical treatment.

questions.s: A 17-year-old boy had frontal headache and nasal discharge for 3 weeks. He now has a soft, tender, doughy swelling in the middle of the forehead above the eyebrows with fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A tender, doughy forehead swelling with fever after frontal sinusitis is Pott puffy tumour, a subperiosteal abscess with osteomyelitis of the frontal bone. It can spread intracranially, so it needs CT, IV antibiotics and surgical drainage. A mucocele usually expands slowly, pushing the eye down and out, without acute infection.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has a soft, painless, smooth swelling in the midline of the neck just below the hyoid bone. It moves upward when he sticks out his tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A midline neck swelling near the hyoid that rises on tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst, because its tract is attached to the foramen caecum of the tongue. It is excised with the central part of the hyoid bone (Sistrunk operation) to prevent recurrence. A dermoid cyst does not move with the tongue, and a branchial cyst lies laterally.

questions.s: A 48-year-old woman has difficulty swallowing solids for 4 months and has lost weight. She has had iron deficiency anaemia for years with koilonychia and angular stomatitis. Barium swallow previously showed a post-cricoid web. Which cancer is she at increased risk of?
questions.e: Chronic iron deficiency with dysphagia from a post-cricoid web (Plummer–Vinson or Paterson–Brown-Kelly syndrome), mostly in women, predisposes to squamous carcinoma of the post-cricoid hypopharynx and upper oesophagus. Lower oesophageal adenocarcinoma is linked to reflux and Barrett oesophagus, not webs.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy has fever and ear pain for a day, with a red, bulging right tympanic membrane. Which bacterium is the most common cause of this condition?
questions.e: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of acute otitis media, followed by non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis, which is why amoxicillin is first line. Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus are typical of otitis externa and chronic discharging ears rather than acute middle ear infection.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl has had bilateral otitis media with effusion confirmed on two visits 3 months apart. Audiometry shows a 30 dB conductive loss in both ears, and her teacher reports poor speech and progress at school. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Persistent bilateral glue ear for 3 months with significant hearing loss and effects on speech or learning is an indication for ventilation tubes (grommets), or hearing aids as an alternative. Antibiotics, antihistamines and decongestants do not clear the effusion. Further waiting is reasonable only when hearing loss is mild and has no impact.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has had intense itching and a blocked right ear for 2 weeks after using antibiotic ear drops for a month. The canal contains wet, white debris speckled with black dots, like damp blotting paper. The drum is intact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Itching and wet white debris with black spores after prolonged antibiotic drops is otomycosis, commonly from Aspergillus niger, treated by careful cleaning of the canal and a topical antifungal such as clotrimazole. More antibiotic drops encourage fungal overgrowth. Steroids have no role and oral antibiotics do not treat fungi.

questions.s: A 20-year-old man has had a foul-smelling right ear discharge for years. For a week he has had severe headache, vomiting and fever of 38 °C. He is drowsy, and fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the brain
Plain X-rays of both mastoids and the skull
questions.e: Headache, vomiting, fever, drowsiness and papilloedema in a patient with chronic ear disease suggest an otogenic brain abscess in the temporal lobe or cerebellum, which needs urgent contrast imaging. Lumbar puncture is dangerous with raised intracranial pressure from a mass because it can cause herniation. Plain mastoid films add little.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has severe pain in the left ear for 2 days, worse on chewing. There is a small, red, tender swelling in the outer part of the ear canal with a central point of pus. Hearing is normal. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.e: A localised, very tender swelling in the outer (cartilaginous) part of the canal is a furuncle, an infection of a hair follicle, and Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause. Pseudomonas typically causes diffuse otitis externa, and Haemophilus is a cause of acute otitis media rather than canal infection.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man has a blocked right ear with reduced hearing for a week. Otoscopy shows hard wax filling the canal. He had a mastoid operation on the right side 10 years ago and has an open mastoid cavity. Which treatment should be avoided?
o: Olive oil drops for a week
Removal with a wax hook under direct vision
questions.e: Ear irrigation should be avoided in anyone with a perforation, previous ear surgery or a mastoid cavity, because water can enter the middle ear or cavity and cause infection or vertigo. Wax in such ears is removed by microsuction or instruments under direct vision, after softening drops if needed.

questions.s: A 22-year-old wrestler from Gujranwala has a tense, fluctuant swelling over the front of his right pinna after a bout 1 day ago. It obliterates the normal contours of the ear. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Cold compresses and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Blood collecting between the perichondrium and cartilage after blunt trauma is an auricular haematoma, and it must be drained promptly and a pressure dressing applied, because the cartilage loses its blood supply and becomes deformed (cauliflower ear). Waiting allows fibrosis and permanent deformity.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has bilateral conductive hearing loss with normal drums. Tympanometry is normal (type A) and stapedial reflexes are absent. What audiometric feature is classically seen in her most likely diagnosis?
o: A notch in air conduction at 4 kHz
A dip in bone conduction at about 2 kHz
A flat sensorineural loss of 90 dB
questions.e: Conductive loss with a normal drum, normal middle ear pressure and absent stapedial reflexes suggests otosclerosis, where stapes fixation produces an apparent dip in bone conduction around 2 kHz called the Carhart notch. A notch at 4 kHz is typical of noise damage, and a low-frequency sensorineural loss suggests Ménière disease.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man has confirmed otosclerosis with a 40 dB conductive loss in his left ear. He does not want to wear a hearing aid. Which operation is most appropriate?
questions.e: Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate, and stapedotomy with a piston prosthesis restores sound transmission to the inner ear, with a hearing aid as the non-surgical alternative. Grommets treat middle ear effusion, mastoidectomy treats infection or cholesteatoma, and cochlear implants are for profound sensorineural loss.

questions.s: A 1-year-old child has bilateral cataracts, a patent ductus arteriosus and does not respond to sounds. His mother had a fever with a rash in early pregnancy. What type of hearing loss is most likely?
questions.e: Congenital rubella syndrome causes the triad of cataract, cardiac defects such as patent ductus arteriosus and sensorineural deafness, which is the commonest single defect. Infection in the first trimester damages the developing cochlea. The middle ear is not primarily affected, so the loss is not conductive.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl is recovering from pneumococcal meningitis treated in a Peshawar hospital. Her parents ask what follow-up is needed before discharge. Which test is most important to arrange early?
questions.e: Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common lasting complication of bacterial meningitis, and every child should have a hearing test soon after recovery because the cochlea can ossify, making cochlear implantation harder if it is delayed. EEG is needed only if seizures persist, and the heart and kidneys are not usually affected.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy has profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss confirmed on brainstem testing. He has worn powerful hearing aids for 6 months without any useful speech development. Imaging shows normal cochleae and auditory nerves. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Children with profound bilateral sensorineural loss who gain little from hearing aids are candidates for cochlear implants, which stimulate the auditory nerve directly; earlier implantation gives better speech outcomes. Bone-anchored aids help conductive or single-sided loss, and stapedotomy and grommets treat middle ear problems.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy had painful bilateral swelling in front of the ears with fever 3 weeks ago. Since then his mother notices he does not hear on the left side. Otoscopy is normal and Weber lateralises to the right. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Mumps parotitis can be followed by a sudden, usually unilateral and often permanent sensorineural hearing loss; Weber moving to the good side with a normal ear canal and drum confirms a sensorineural cause. Wax, glue ear and perforations cause conductive loss, which would send Weber to the affected ear and show abnormal otoscopy.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy had a cleft palate repaired at 1 year. His mother reports poor hearing and he has had recurrent ear infections. Why is he especially prone to middle ear effusion?
questions.e: Tensor veli palatini opens the Eustachian tube on swallowing, and in cleft palate its insertion is abnormal, so the tube fails to ventilate the middle ear and effusion is very common. The cochlea and ear canal are usually normal. Children with cleft palate need regular hearing checks.

questions.s: A 47-year-old shopkeeper has a confirmed diagnosis of Ménière disease with attacks every few weeks. Which long-term measure is most appropriate first?
questions.e: Initial prevention of Ménière attacks uses lifestyle measures, especially reducing salt, and betahistine, which is widely used to reduce attack frequency. Vestibular sedatives such as prochlorperazine are for short-term control of acute attacks only. Destructive procedures such as labyrinthectomy are reserved for disabling disease with poor hearing, and the Epley manoeuvre treats BPPV.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman developed severe continuous vertigo with vomiting 2 days after an upper respiratory infection. She also noticed muffled hearing and tinnitus in her right ear. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows a right sensorineural loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute continuous vertigo with new sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus after a viral illness indicates labyrinthitis, which affects both the vestibular and cochlear parts of the inner ear. Vestibular neuritis affects only the vestibular nerve, so hearing is normal. BPPV causes brief positional attacks and a schwannoma progresses slowly.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman has seconds-long spinning when she lies down or rolls over in bed. A doctor wants to confirm the suspected diagnosis at the bedside. Which test should be performed?
questions.e: Brief vertigo triggered by lying down or rolling over is typical of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, and the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces it with a characteristic torsional nystagmus after a short delay. Romberg and Unterberger tests are non-specific tests of balance, and Weber is a hearing test.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man has been diagnosed with vestibular neuritis. After 4 days the vomiting has stopped, but he still feels unsteady when moving his head. He has been taking prochlorperazine regularly. What is the most appropriate advice now?
o: Stop the sedative and begin vestibular exercises
Continue regular prochlorperazine for 3 more months
Bed rest with the head still until symptoms go
Start betahistine and avoid all head movements
questions.e: Vestibular sedatives help in the first few days of severe vertigo, but continuing them delays central compensation. Once vomiting settles, the patient should stop them and begin vestibular rehabilitation with graded head and eye movement exercises, which speed recovery. Bed rest and avoiding movement have the same harmful effect on compensation.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman with a large vestibular schwannoma in the right cerebellopontine angle has right sensorineural hearing loss. As the tumour grows, which cranial nerve is usually next affected, giving a reduced corneal reflex?
questions.e: As a vestibular schwannoma enlarges in the cerebellopontine angle it compresses the trigeminal nerve, and a reduced corneal reflex is an early sign. The facial nerve, though close by, tolerates stretching well, so obvious facial weakness is late. The abducens and lower cranial nerves are involved only by very large tumours.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man has a left Bell palsy. He says ordinary sounds such as doors closing are uncomfortably loud in his left ear. Paralysis of which muscle explains this?
questions.e: The facial nerve supplies stapedius, which damps stapes movement in response to loud sound, so its paralysis causes hyperacusis. Tensor tympani is supplied by the mandibular nerve and is spared in Bell palsy. Hyperacusis therefore suggests the lesion is at or above the nerve to stapedius.

questions.s: A 25-year-old motorcyclist hit the left side of his head in a road accident. He has bruising behind the left ear, blood behind the left drum and a left conductive hearing loss. Facial movements are normal. Which injury is most likely?
o: Longitudinal fracture of the temporal bone
Transverse fracture of the temporal bone
questions.e: Longitudinal temporal bone fractures are the more common type and run along the external canal and middle ear, causing haemotympanum and conductive loss, with facial palsy less often. Transverse fractures cross the otic capsule and typically cause sensorineural deafness, vertigo and facial palsy. Bruising behind the ear (Battle sign) indicates a skull base fracture.

questions.s: The vascular plexus in Little's area on the anterior nasal septum receives blood from both the external and internal carotid systems. Which contributing artery is a branch of the internal carotid system?
questions.e: The anterior ethmoidal artery comes from the ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid, while the sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries all arise from the external carotid system. This dual supply is why ligation of a single artery may not stop bleeding.

questions.s: A 9-year-old girl has frequent small nosebleeds from the left nostril, usually after picking. Examination shows crusting and prominent vessels on the left anterior septum. Bleeding stops easily with pressure. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Silver nitrate cautery to both sides of the septum
questions.e: Recurrent minor anterior nosebleeds in children are usually caused by crusting and vestibulitis over Little's area, and an antiseptic cream applied to the nasal vestibule for 2 weeks is the first treatment. Cautery is used if bleeding continues, but never on both sides of the septum at once because of the risk of perforation.

questions.s: A 63-year-old carpenter has had left nasal blockage and blood-stained discharge for 3 months. Recently he has numbness over the left cheek and his left upper teeth feel loose. What is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Allergy skin prick testing and serum IgE level
CT of the sinuses and endoscopic biopsy
questions.e: Unilateral nasal obstruction with blood-stained discharge, cheek numbness (infraorbital nerve) and loose upper teeth in an older woodworker strongly suggest a sinonasal malignancy such as adenocarcinoma of the ethmoid or maxilla. CT shows bone destruction and extent, and endoscopic biopsy confirms the diagnosis. Plain films and swabs are inadequate.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man arrives in the emergency room with heavy bleeding from the nose for 3 hours. He is pale and sweaty, BP 88/60 mmHg and pulse 124/min. What is the first priority?
o: Insert a posterior nasal pack in the emergency room
Obtain IV access and start fluid resuscitation
questions.e: Like any haemorrhage, severe epistaxis is managed by resuscitation first: this man is shocked, so wide-bore IV access, bloods for cross-match and fluid replacement come before local measures. Packing and cautery follow once he is stable, with first aid pressure maintained meanwhile. Imaging is not part of initial care.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man had posterior epistaxis controlled with a posterior pack, but it restarted heavily each time the pack was removed over 3 days. Clotting and platelets are normal. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
o: External carotid artery ligation in the neck
Daily oral tranexamic acid for a month
questions.e: Posterior epistaxis that recurs despite packing is best controlled by endoscopic ligation or cautery of the sphenopalatine artery, which supplies most of the posterior nasal cavity; embolisation is an alternative. External carotid ligation is too proximal and fails because of collateral flow, and septoplasty does not address the bleeding vessel.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has had nosebleeds and bruises on his legs for 2 days. Two weeks ago he had a viral fever. He is well, with no lymph nodes or spleen enlargement. Hb 12.2 g/dL, white cells 7.5 × 10⁹/L with normal differential, platelets 12 × 10⁹/L (150–400). Blood film shows large platelets only. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with large platelets and otherwise normal counts in a well child after a viral illness is immune thrombocytopenia, which usually resolves on its own. Leukaemia and aplastic anaemia affect other cell lines, and haemophilia causes joint and muscle bleeds with a normal platelet count.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has had nasal blockage, clear-to-yellow discharge and mild facial ache for 4 days with a cold. Temperature is 37.6 °C. She has no eye swelling or severe headache. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral amoxicillin for 7 days with a decongestant spray
questions.e: Short-lived sinus symptoms with a cold are almost always viral rhinosinusitis, which settles without antibiotics; analgesia, saline irrigation and reassurance are appropriate. Antibiotics are considered if symptoms last more than about 10 days or worsen after initial improvement. Imaging is for complications or chronic disease.

questions.s: A 15-year-old girl has had right-sided nasal blockage for 8 months. Examination shows a single smooth, pale, pedunculated polyp in the right nasal cavity, and on looking at the back of the mouth it can be seen hanging behind the soft palate. From where does this polyp usually arise?
questions.e: A unilateral solitary polyp in a young person that extends backward into the choana and nasopharynx is an antrochoanal polyp, which arises from the maxillary sinus mucosa and passes through its ostium. It is removed endoscopically along with its antral part to prevent recurrence. Ethmoidal polyps are usually multiple and bilateral.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman with asthma and bilateral nasal polyps had a severe asthma attack within an hour of taking a painkiller for a headache. Which group of drugs should she avoid?
questions.e: Asthma, nasal polyps and sensitivity to aspirin form aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter triad); cyclo-oxygenase inhibition shifts arachidonic acid towards leukotrienes and triggers bronchospasm, so aspirin and NSAIDs must be avoided. Paracetamol at usual doses is generally tolerated, and intranasal steroids are a mainstay of polyp treatment.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy has bilateral nasal polyps. He also has recurrent chest infections with productive cough and is below the 3rd centile for weight. His stools are bulky and greasy. Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.e: Nasal polyps are rare in children, and with recurrent chest infections, poor growth and steatorrhoea they strongly suggest cystic fibrosis, confirmed by a raised sweat chloride. Allergy tests and IgE assess atopy, which does not explain malabsorption and failure to thrive.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman from a poor area of Hyderabad has thick greenish crusts in both nasal cavities with a very offensive smell that others notice, though she cannot smell it herself. The nasal cavities look abnormally roomy with shrunken turbinates. Which organism is classically associated with this condition?
questions.e: Roomy nasal cavities with atrophic turbinates, foul crusts and anosmia (so the patient is unaware of the smell) describe atrophic rhinitis (ozaena), classically associated with Klebsiella ozaenae. Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis causes rhinoscleroma with nodular granulomas, and Rhinosporidium causes bleeding strawberry-like polyps.

questions.s: A 21-year-old man was hit on the nose during a football match yesterday. His nose is swollen and appears deviated to the left. He can breathe through both nostrils, and the septum looks straight with no swelling. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Review in 5–7 days once swelling settles
questions.e: After a nasal fracture without septal haematoma, review at about 5 to 7 days, when swelling has settled, allows proper assessment of deformity; closed reduction, if needed, is done within about 2 weeks before the bones set. Nasal X-rays do not change management. Delayed septorhinoplasty is for deformity missed or untreated in this window.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man has had worsening nasal blockage for 2 months. He has been using a decongestant nasal spray several times a day for this period because it gives relief for a few hours. The nasal mucosa is red and swollen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prolonged use of topical decongestants such as xylometazoline causes rebound vasodilatation and congestion, called rhinitis medicamentosa, so the patient uses the spray more and more. Treatment is to stop the decongestant, usually with an intranasal steroid to cover the withdrawal. Polyps are pale and do not explain the history.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man had a head injury in a road accident a week ago. He now has a constant clear, watery drip from his right nostril that increases when he bends forward. Which test on the fluid best confirms its origin?
questions.e: Watery rhinorrhoea after head injury that increases on bending forward suggests a CSF leak through a skull base fracture, and beta-2 transferrin, found in CSF but not in nasal mucus or serum, confirms it. Glucose dipsticks are unreliable because nasal secretions can contain glucose and blood contamination gives false positives.

questions.s: A 12-year-old girl's mother asks whether her daughter needs her tonsils removed. Which history most clearly meets the usual criteria for tonsillectomy?
o: Two sore throats a year for 3 years
Seven well-documented episodes of tonsillitis in the past year
One episode of tonsillitis with fever and a hospital admission last month
Large tonsils seen on routine examination
questions.e: Commonly used criteria for tonsillectomy in recurrent tonsillitis are 7 or more significant episodes in 1 year, 5 a year for 2 years, or 3 a year for 3 years, with episodes disabling enough to affect school or work. Large tonsils without symptoms are not an indication, and occasional sore throats do not justify the risks of surgery.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy had a tonsillectomy this morning. Six hours later he vomits fresh blood, there is a clot in the left tonsillar fossa, and his pulse is 130/min despite IV fluids and pressure with a swab. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Return to theatre to control the bleeding
Give oral tranexamic acid and discharge
Apply an ice pack to the neck
questions.e: Bleeding within 24 hours of tonsillectomy is reactionary haemorrhage, often from a slipped tie or a vessel opening as blood pressure recovers. Tachycardia and continued bleeding despite simple measures require urgent return to theatre to secure the vessel. Antibiotics are the main treatment for secondary haemorrhage from infection at 5 to 10 days.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has had discomfort on swallowing and pain in his right ear for 2 months. The right tonsil is much larger than the left and has an ulcer with a hard edge. There is a firm, painless node at the right angle of the jaw. The ear is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure as asymmetric tonsils are common
questions.e: A unilaterally enlarged, ulcerated, firm tonsil with referred otalgia (via the glossopharyngeal nerve) and a firm neck node in an older adult suggests tonsillar carcinoma or lymphoma, so biopsy is needed. Antibiotics only delay diagnosis, and there is no pus to aspirate. Asymmetry with these features is never simply reassured.

questions.s: A 23-year-old university student who has been under stress and neglecting his teeth has painful, bleeding gums, foul breath, fever and a greyish ulcer on one tonsil. Smear shows fusiform bacilli and spirochaetes. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Topical steroid paste applied after meals
questions.e: Ulcerative tonsillitis with necrotising gingivitis, halitosis and a smear of fusiform bacilli and spirochaetes is Vincent angina, an anaerobic infection linked to poor oral hygiene, treated with penicillin and metronidazole plus oral hygiene. Fluconazole treats candidiasis, and aciclovir is for herpes infections.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man has regurgitated undigested food eaten hours earlier, a gurgling sound in the neck on swallowing, bad breath and recurrent coughing at night. He has lost a little weight. Which investigation is most appropriate first?
questions.e: Regurgitation of old food, gurgling in the neck, halitosis and aspiration in an older person suggest a pharyngeal (Zenker) pouch, best shown by a barium swallow. Blind endoscopy risks entering and perforating the pouch, so contrast imaging comes first. Manometry is used for motility disorders such as achalasia.

questions.s: An 18-month-old boy has a barking cough and stridor. The doctor explains that this is a common viral illness of the larynx and trachea. Which virus is the most common cause?
questions.e: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is most often caused by parainfluenza viruses, which inflame the subglottis and cause the barking cough and stridor. Respiratory syncytial virus is the main cause of bronchiolitis in infants, EBV causes infectious mononucleosis, and rotavirus causes diarrhoea.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl with croup has stridor at rest, marked subcostal recession and is agitated. Oxygen saturation is 93 % in air. She received oral dexamethasone 20 minutes ago. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Severe croup with stridor at rest, recession and agitation needs nebulised adrenaline, which rapidly reduces mucosal swelling while the steroid takes effect, plus oxygen and senior review. Its effect wears off in a few hours, so she must be observed. Salbutamol acts on lower airway bronchospasm, and antibiotics do not treat viral croup.

questions.s: A health visitor in a Sindh village explains to a mother why her baby needs the pentavalent vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. Which life-threatening airway infection of childhood does this vaccine largely prevent?
questions.e: The pentavalent vaccine in Pakistan's EPI schedule includes Haemophilus influenzae type b, the classic cause of acute epiglottitis, which has become rare where Hib vaccination is high. Croup is viral, retropharyngeal abscess is mixed bacterial, and laryngomalacia is a developmental condition.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman is extubated after a total thyroidectomy for a large goitre. Within minutes she develops marked inspiratory stridor and distress, but her voice is fairly normal. Laryngoscopy shows both vocal cords lying close to the midline and not moving apart on inspiration. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Both cords fixed near the midline after thyroidectomy indicate bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy; the voice may be near normal but the narrow glottis causes stridor, and she needs reintubation or tracheostomy. External laryngeal nerve injury affects pitch, not airway. Hypocalcaemia appears a day or more later and does not fix the cords.

questions.s: A 64-year-old smoker has had a hoarse voice for 6 weeks with weight loss. Chest X-ray shows a mass at the left hilum. Laryngoscopy shows a paralysed left vocal cord. Why is the left side more often affected than the right in chest disease?
o: The left nerve hooks around the arch of the aorta
The left nerve runs with the left phrenic nerve
The left nerve hooks around the subclavian artery
The left nerve passes through the left lung root
questions.e: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus in the thorax and loops under the aortic arch, so lung cancer at the left hilum, mediastinal nodes, aortic aneurysm or a large left atrium can compress it. The right nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery in the neck root and so has a shorter, less exposed course.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl has had a progressively hoarse voice for a year and recently some noisy breathing. Laryngoscopy shows multiple warty, exophytic growths on both vocal cords. The lesions recurred within months after laser removal. Which agent causes this condition?
questions.e: Multiple warty laryngeal lesions in a child that recur after removal are recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, caused by HPV types 6 and 11, often acquired from the mother at birth. EBV is linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and laryngeal tuberculosis causes ulceration in adults with lung disease rather than recurrent warts.

questions.s: A 32-year-old primary school teacher has a hoarse, breathy voice that worsens through the week. Laryngoscopy shows small, symmetrical swellings on both vocal cords at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two-thirds. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
o: Voice therapy with a speech therapist
Microlaryngeal surgery to remove both nodules
questions.e: Bilateral symmetrical nodules at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the cords are vocal (singer's) nodules from voice overuse, and most respond to voice therapy and vocal hygiene. Surgery is reserved for nodules that persist despite therapy. They are benign, so radiotherapy has no role.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy swallowed a coin an hour ago and has mild discomfort when swallowing but no breathing difficulty. An X-ray shows a round coin seen face-on at the level of the thoracic inlet. Where do swallowed coins most commonly lodge in children?
questions.e: The cricopharyngeal sphincter is the narrowest point of the gut and the most common site for swallowed coins to lodge in children, appearing at the thoracic inlet. A coin in the oesophagus is seen face-on in an AP view, whereas one in the trachea is usually seen edge-on. The aortic arch and gastro-oesophageal junction are less common sites.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl pushed a small button battery into her right nostril 2 hours ago. She is comfortable and breathing normally. The battery is visible in the anterior nasal cavity. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Saline drops to wash it out at home
questions.e: Button batteries in the nose cause electrical and chemical burns within hours, leading to septal perforation, so they need urgent removal. Saline drops increase the current and worsen injury. Delayed review or simple observation risks serious tissue damage.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has been unable to swallow even his saliva for 4 hours since a piece of meat stuck while eating. He is drooling but breathing comfortably. He has had intermittent food sticking for a year. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Discharge with advice to drink fizzy drinks
Urgent flexible endoscopy to remove the bolus
Oral proton pump inhibitor and review
questions.e: Complete oesophageal obstruction with inability to swallow saliva risks aspiration and pressure necrosis, so the bolus should be removed by urgent endoscopy, which also shows any underlying stricture or eosinophilic oesophagitis. Barium makes later endoscopy difficult. Waiting for the bolus to pass is reasonable only if saliva can be swallowed.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy has a plastic bead in his right nostril, clearly visible near the front. He is cooperative and his mother is with him. Which method is most appropriate to try first?
o: Flushing the nose with water through a syringe
Parent blowing into his mouth (parent's kiss)
questions.e: For a visible anterior nasal foreign body in a cooperative child, positive-pressure methods such as the 'parent's kiss', where the parent blows into the mouth while blocking the other nostril, are simple, painless and often successful. Grasping a smooth round bead with forceps tends to push it further back, and flushing risks aspiration. General anaesthesia is kept for failure.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl has a small round plastic bead in her left ear canal. It is smooth and fills most of the canal lumen. What is the best way to remove it?
o: Pass a blunt hook beyond it and pull out
Leave it to fall out naturally
questions.e: Smooth, round objects slip out of forceps jaws and are pushed deeper towards the drum, so they are removed with a blunt right-angled hook passed beyond the object, or with suction, under direct vision. Forceps suit soft or irregular objects such as paper or cotton. Plastic does not dissolve and will not fall out on its own.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man was drinking heavily and inhaled a peanut. He now has cough and fever. A CT scan shows an obstructed bronchus with collapse and consolidation beyond it. In which part of the lungs does an aspirated foreign body most often lodge in an upright adult?
questions.e: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled objects most often enter it, and in an upright person they fall into the right lower lobe bronchi. Upper lobes are involved mainly when aspiration occurs lying down.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man has had a painless, firm lump in the left upper neck for 6 weeks. He smokes and chews naswar. There is no infection in the throat or teeth. What is the most appropriate initial investigation of the lump?
o: Two-week course of oral antibiotics and review
questions.e: A persistent neck lump in an adult smoker may be a metastatic squamous carcinoma node, and ultrasound with fine needle aspiration cytology is the first investigation, followed by a full examination of the upper aerodigestive tract for a primary. Open excision of the node first can seed tumour and compromise later surgery.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man has a smooth, painless, fluctuant swelling in the right side of the neck that has slowly enlarged over a year. It lies deep to the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the junction of its upper and middle thirds. Aspiration yields turbid fluid. What does microscopy of this fluid typically show?
questions.e: A cystic swelling at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in a young adult is a branchial cyst, and its fluid typically contains cholesterol crystals. Acid-fast bacilli would suggest tuberculous lymphadenitis, which is common in Pakistan but usually presents as matted nodes, and Reed–Sternberg cells indicate Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.s: A 3-month-old baby has a large, soft, painless swelling in the left posterior triangle of the neck since birth. It is compressible and lights up brightly when a torch is held against it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A soft, compressible, brilliantly transilluminant swelling in the posterior triangle of an infant is a cystic hygroma, a lymphatic malformation. A sternocleidomastoid tumour is a firm mass within the muscle with torticollis, and a branchial cyst usually presents in young adults and is not brightly transilluminant.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has painful swelling under the left side of his jaw that comes on every time he eats and settles over an hour. The swelling is firm when present. A hard object can be felt in the floor of the mouth on the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Swelling and pain of the submandibular gland at meals with a palpable hard object in the floor of the mouth is a stone in the submandibular (Wharton) duct, the commonest site for salivary stones because its secretion is thick and its duct runs upward. Mumps causes constant bilateral parotid swelling, and a pleomorphic adenoma is painless.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man from Karachi has chewed areca nut (chalia) daily since school. He has a burning sensation with spicy food and can now open his mouth only 2 cm. The buccal mucosa is pale and marble-like with palpable vertical fibrous bands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Areca nut chewing with burning on spicy food, blanched mucosa, palpable fibrous bands and progressive trismus is oral submucous fibrosis, a potentially malignant disorder. The patient should stop areca nut and be followed for oral cancer. Lichen planus shows white lace-like striae, and candidiasis gives wipeable white plaques without trismus.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man has a small squamous cell carcinoma confined to the middle of the right vocal cord with normal cord movement. The surgeon tells him that spread to neck nodes is unlikely at this stage. What is the reason?
o: The cords are covered by columnar epithelium
Neck nodes are removed by radiotherapy
questions.e: The true vocal cords have very sparse lymphatic drainage, so early glottic carcinomas rarely spread to neck nodes and are often cured by radiotherapy or laser surgery. Supraglottic cancers have rich lymphatics and spread to nodes early. The cords are covered by stratified squamous epithelium, not columnar.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man who has smoked for 50 years has painless, soft swellings at the angle of the jaw on both sides, slowly growing for 2 years. Facial nerve function is normal. Fine needle aspiration shows oncocytic epithelial cells and lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Warthin tumour (adenolymphoma) typically affects the lower pole of the parotid in older male smokers, may be bilateral, and shows oncocytic epithelium with lymphoid stroma on cytology. Pleomorphic adenoma is usually single and shows chondromyxoid stroma. Malignancy would more likely cause pain or facial weakness.
